The wobble hypothesis explains the degeneracy of the genetic code.
The wobble hypothesis states that codon-anticodon pairing follows the traditional Watson—Crick
tules (G pairs with C and A pairs with U) for the first two bases of the codon but can be less
stringent for the third/last base. It has been observed that a tRNA can recognize more than one
codon for a specific amino acid, especially in the last nucleotide of the codon triplet. This is
referred to as degeneracy and its mechanism can be explained by the wobble hypothesis.
The first base of the anticodon moves to permit nontraditional pairing with the last base of the
codon. This movement is called wobble and is possible because the first base of the anticodon is
not as spatially defined as the other two bases. Due to the wobbling, 61 tRNA species are not
required to read the 61 codons.
For example, three codons for glycine—GGU, GGC, and GGA—can form a base pair from one

Equilibrium potential for an ion is calculated using the Nernst equation.
When there is a concentration gradient for an ion across the membrane, the ion tends to diffuse down the concentration gradient. The electric potential that exactly opposes this net diffusion is called the equilibrium potential for that ion. This is calculated using the Nernst equation.
It is expressed as the potential inside the cell (intracellular potential relative to the extracellular potential).
To calculate the value of the equilibrium potential:
Nernst equation
EMF (millivolts) = ±(61/z) × log(Concentration inside / Concentration outside)
Note: In this formula, the choice of concentration of the ion placed in the numerator and denominator does not matter because the formula is only used to derive the numerical value and not the sign (+/-). Mathematically, log(100/10) = 1 and log(10/100) = -1. Hence, changing the numerator and denominator only changes the sign and the numerical value remains the same.
This equation is used only to derive the numerical value of the potential. It is NOT used to derive the sign/charge (+/-).
The sign/charge is derived from logic:
• In a positive (+) ion, if the concentration of the + ion is greater outside, then the + ion moves from outside to inside. The intracellular potential becomes more positive relatively. Hence, the potential will be positive.
• In a positive (+) ion, if the concentration of the + ion is greater inside, then the + ion moves from inside to outside. The intracellular potential becomes more negative relatively (as + ion moves outside). Hence the potential will be negative.
• In a negative (-) ion, if the concentration of the - ion is greater outside, then the - ion moves from outside to inside. The intracellular potential becomes more negative relatively. Hence the potential will be negative.
• In a negative (-) ion, if the concentration of the - ion is greater inside, then the - ion moves from inside to outside. The intracellular potential becomes more positive relatively (as - ion moves outside). Hence the potential will be positive.

Memory is of 3 types:
• Immediate
• Recent

Immediate memory is attention dependent. Tests of attention and memory include

• Days of the week backwards

Digit span test

The examiner recites numbers randomly without any sequence and asks the patient to repeat the same. The examiner starts with a 2-number sequence and the digit span increases from 2 numbers to 3 numbers and so on. The patient is asked to repeat until he/she fails to repeat all numbers correctly.

Digit forward
• Normally a person can repeat up to 7 digits (+/- 2).
• E.g., Examiner says 2 - 4 - 8 - 1 - 5 - 7 - 9. The person has to repeat in the same order 2 - 4 - 8 - 1 - 5 - 7 - 9.

Digit backward
• Reproduction of longer digits in backward direction.
• Normally a person can repeat up to 5 digits (+/- 1) in backward direction (making option C wrong).
• Eg: Examiner says 2 - 4 - 8 - 1 - 5 - 7 - 9. The person has to repeat it backwards. 9 - 7 - 5 - 1 - 8 - 4 - 2.

Serial (100-7) subtraction test
• 5 scores / steps are taken in to account.
• 1st score – When the patient tells 93 (100 - 7 = 93).
• 2nd score - When the patient tells 86 (93 – 7 = 86).
• And so on . . 100 , 93 , 86 , 79 , 72 , 65.

Hence among the given options:

Digit span forward up to 7 digits with 2 skips allowed would be the answer of choice as it is the best test for immediate memory.
